objective: Prevent a lost update with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a single atomic UPDATE, and compare isolation levels
secondaryObjectives: Group statements into a transaction with BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT, and explain atomicity

sources.note: Relevant text (Read Committed): an UPDATE that finds its target row already changed by a concurrent transaction 'will wait for the first updating transaction to commit or roll back' and then 'the WHERE clause is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches'; the example 'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100.00 WHERE acctnum = 12345' is safe because 'each command is affecting only a predetermined row'. (Repeatable Read): if a concurrent updater commits, the transaction 'will be rolled back with the message ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update', and the application should 'abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning'. Read through a summarizing fetch of the PostgreSQL 18.7 page on 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: 'FOR UPDATE causes the rows retrieved by the SELECT statement to be locked as though for update. This prevents them from being locked, modified or deleted by other transactions until the current transaction ends.' Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-14. Why a read-then-write inside one transaction with FOR UPDATE does not lose updates.

Relevant text: BEGIN starts a transaction block, COMMIT makes its changes visible together and ROLLBACK discards them. Read in full as raw HTML on 2026-11-14 for the course (REQ-265); the course's key value is used here.

brief.situation: You are the database engineer at Fernhill Books, a fictional online bookshop. At 10:00 the signed edition of 'Harbor Lights' (book 4711, 500 copies printed) went on sale. At 10:12 the warehouse reports 537 orders for it, while the stock column still says 41 copies are left, and orders keep coming at about six a minute. Stop the overselling, find why concurrent checkouts lose stock updates, get a correct fix deployed, prove it under concurrency, and put the book back on sale.
handover: The checkout developer is standing by to deploy whichever change you choose (about 6 minutes each). The database is PostgreSQL 18 at its default isolation level.
A staging copy has a race test that sends 50 concurrent buyers at 10 remaining copies.
Customer service, not you, handles the customers who were oversold. Paid orders must not be deleted.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments come from its list.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The incident keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, service or job and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why concurrent checkouts sold more copies than existed, what you did first, which fix you chose over the alternatives and how you proved it.

parts.label: The cause
parts.criteria: Names a lost update: two transactions read the same stock, each computes a new value and the second write overwrites the first; Read Committed does not prevent it for a read-then-write.
parts.modelAnswer: Checkout ran SELECT stock, computed stock - qty in the application and wrote the number back. Two buyers reading 41 at once both wrote 40, so one sale was never subtracted. At Read Committed nothing stops that.

parts.label: Containment and the fix
parts.criteria: Took the book off sale first; chose a single conditional UPDATE (stock = stock - qty WHERE stock >= qty) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction; explains why Repeatable Read without retries, a table lock, a CHECK constraint, resetting stock or deleting orders are wrong here.
parts.modelAnswer: I took 4711 off sale, then had checkout use UPDATE books SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock >= $1: the row update re-checks the condition on the latest version, so a buyer gets 0 rows when it has sold out. Repeatable Read would turn races into errors unless the app retries; a table lock serializes every checkout; the CHECK never fires because the app never writes a negative.

parts.label: Proof
parts.criteria: Ran a concurrency test (the race test) after the fix and only then reopened the sale.
parts.modelAnswer: The staging race test accepted exactly 10 of 50 buyers for 10 copies with stock ending at 0; then I put the book back on sale.

expertPath.text: Take book 4711 off sale: one statement stops the bleeding while you investigate.
Count what was sold against the 500 printed; pg_stat_statements shows SELECT stock then UPDATE ... SET stock = $1: a read-then-write at Read Committed, a lost update.
Deploy a single conditional UPDATE (stock = stock - qty WHERE stock >= qty, 0 rows means sold out), or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the transaction.
Race test on staging: exactly 10 of 50 accepted. Reopen the sale. Leave the oversold customers to customer service with an accurate count; delete nothing.

scoring.modelReasoning: Checkout read stock, subtracted in the application and wrote the number back. Two concurrent buyers read the same value and the second write erased the first: a lost update, which Read Committed allows. Stop the selling first, then decrement in one statement with a condition (UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - qty WHERE id = ... AND stock >= qty), whose row update re-checks the condition on the newest row version, or lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the transaction. Repeatable Read also stops it only if the application retries serialization failures; a table lock queues every checkout. Prove it with concurrent buyers, then reopen.
